summary: Pleasant Bay light off South Addison, Maine: first lit 1838, present brick tower from the 1870s. Automated 1947, discontinued 1982, now owned by volunteers.

structures.note: First tower, 24 feet, built on a ledge (LighthouseFriends). Its later fate is not stated in the sources read.
Present tower; LighthouseFriends dates it to 1873, the Society's record to 1874. Base to lantern 29 feet.

access.note: Not open to the public (Society record). Island closed April through August; grounds open seasonally; tower closed (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.proposed: square brick tower, built 1874 (LighthouseFriends: 1873); first rubblestone tower built 1838
corrections.why: The 1838 tower was the first. The brick tower standing today is the 1873-1874 tower, per the Society's record and LighthouseFriends.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The present tower is dated 1873 by LighthouseFriends, which also reports the 1873 Act of Congress for rebuilding the upper part of the tower. The Society's record gives 1874. The story gives both.
LighthouseFriends says a Fresnel lens went into the earlier tower in 1856. The Society's record gives 1874 for the optic in the present tower. Both are kept, for different towers.

The Society's record gives a bell tower built in 1882 and a fog-signal building in 1888, while also saying there is no fog-signal building. LighthouseFriends gives 1887 for the bell tower. The story gives the bell tower's date as the two sources' dates, not a settled date.

notes_for_editor: Roster: 23 archive lines, matched by name only (the archive gives no position for Nash Island); copied as printed. Robert Purington (keeper, 20 December 1920, Bulletin and index) added as a keeper line with no person slug; not on the archive roster. Raymond Purington is named as a son who helped in 1920-21 but is not called keeper anywhere read; not on the roster. The 1838 tower's later fate is not stated in the sources read. LighthouseFriends calls the 1873 brick tower 'the present' tower; the 1873 Act funded rebuilding its upper part; the Society's record dates the present tower to 1874. The Society's record: 1882 bell tower, 1888 fog-signal building yet 'Fog Signal Building? No'. LighthouseFriends: bell tower 1887. Unresolved. The record says tower 9.0 m, USLHS says 29 feet (8.8 m) from base to lantern: a small difference; not corrected. Record focal height 17.4 m agrees with USLHS (57 feet above mean high water). Quotations from LighthouseFriends (the 1850 inspection, the 1872 inspector's letter, Holt's 1892 letter, the Coast Guard fire of about 1947) come from its quotations of National Archives letters and a family member's recollections, which were not checked. They are attributed to LighthouseFriends in the story. The 1916 schooner Maine rescue is cited only to LighthouseFriends. The Commissioner's FY1916 aids table (scan 165) names J. E. Purington with 'Schooner Maine' in OCR columns that do not align; the table is not quoted. The Commissioner's FY1921 report (scan 663) prints the name as 'Purlington' in OCR; read as Purington, the archive and Bulletin spelling. The 1917 Bulletin entry (June 21) gives the freighter's name in garbled OCR; not used. The Commissioner's report and Robert's Bulletin entry (20 December 1920) appear to describe the same tow; stated that way in the story. John E. Purington was an assistant at Egg Rock, Great Duck and Mark Island before 1916 (LighthouseFriends). No dates in the sources read, so no other_stations entries. The 1931 Bulletin mention of a rescue about two miles off Nash Island was by another station and is not used. Private land on the island (family-owned until the 1990s per LighthouseFriends) is not described beyond the refuge status. The family members are not named beyond the Purington sons and the 'daughter' referred to only as the family's child. Coast Guard crew members in LighthouseFriends are not named. Maine newspapers: three searches; one useful page (1873 appropriation). Record position (OSM) 44.464261, -67.74729 vs LighthouseFriends 44.46431, -67.74728: the same place. No women keepers, apart from the family's children, are named as keepers in the sources read. Wikipedia not used. USCG Historian not checked (blocked). No general period context used: the general corpus has no passage on striking fog-bell machines. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the Commissioner's 1921 entry (scan 663, printed p. 58) prints the surname 'Purlington'; checked on the page image, and the story records that spelling. The 1917 freighter's name is read from garbled OCR ('Rocld ancl'); the story says only 'a Rockland freighter' and the page image was not checked for that word. Bulletin PDF pages 35, 7 and index 31 verified.
